extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers and creative-writing students interested in minimalist/Carver-style fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing short stories in the Raymond Carver / minimalism tradition: economical prose, elliptical structure, restrained emotion, and working-class subject matter. Focuses on craft techniques and quality criteria that produce 'less-is-more' literary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Aesthetic — "Less is more"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Less is more." Sparse narrative; simple, straightforward language; more unsaid than said. No elaborate plot or verbose detailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize economy and omission over exposition. Aim for a surface that gestures at deeper meaning rather than explaining it; avoid elaborate plotting and excessive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptical dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters talk past each other; conversations end before they conclude; silences carry weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial exchanges, interruptions, and subtext so dialogue implies more than it states. Allow pauses and non-sequiturs to reveal relationships and tension without explicit explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-jump structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Elliptical transitions between scenes leaving the reader to fill gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skip over unimportant stretches of time or causal exposition. Rely on implication and juxtaposition of moments so readers infer what happens between scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamiliarization
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show common objects, routines, or interactions in ways that reveal new meaning or emotional resonance; small changes of perspective can make everyday details feel charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place scenes, images, or tones next to one another so their contrast produces interpretation; let implication arise from how elements sit side-by-side rather than from explicit commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid neatly resolving narrative or emotional threads. Leave questions open and let the reader inhabit uncertainty; ambiguity should feel deliberate, not careless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition and mirroring (phrases, actions, scene shapes) to build resonance and thematic unity without explicit statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestive imagery
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a few precise, concrete images that carry emotional or symbolic weight; these details should act as focal points that the reader lingers on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pared-back diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Anglo-Saxon over Latinate vocabulary; lean word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, concrete words; eliminate ornate or Latinate synonyms when plain Anglo-Saxon diction will be clearer and more immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withheld interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited access to thoughts; behavior over psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show characters primarily through speech and action rather than internal monologue. Let gestures and dialogue imply inner life instead of explicit exposition of feelings or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working-class subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on bartenders, mechanics, broken marriages, alcoholism and similar blue-collar settings and concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground stories in everyday labor, domestic settings, and economic realities; use social detail to shape character and tone without turning setting into sociology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every word must do work
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate superfluous words; each word should contribute to meaning, tone, image, or plot. This principle drives sentence-level editing and line-by-line pruning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface implies depth (iceberg theory)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt Hemingway's iceberg approach: present only the visible tip while a larger emotional or narrative mass remains unstated. Trust readers to infer the submerged material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader does the meaning-making
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narrative gaps, silences, and implications so readers actively construct significance; avoid over-explaining themes or psychological states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity at moment of action
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise when showing actions or critical moments—specific, concrete details at key instants yield richness without lengthy background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence as eloquence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use omission, pauses, and what is left unsaid as expressive devices. Strategic silence can communicate more powerfully than explicit description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited vocabulary that intensifies attention
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict lexical range intentionally to sharpen focus; repetition of a tighter set of words can increase intensity and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirty Realism characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language, blue-collar settings, emotional reticence, secular grief (term coined by Bill Buford for Carver-school fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace an unadorned register and modest settings that foreground quiet struggle and muted emotion; the label highlights social/material grounding plus restrained tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carver's practical maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Carver's own statements: "Get in. Get out. Don't linger." "Use no superfluous word." A short story is "a glimpse" — small but devastating. The writer must "stand at his own window and see the world freshly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aphorisms summarize the minimalist ethos: enter scenes only as necessary, excise excess, aim for a small but intense effect, and observe the world with renewed attention. Use them as editorial tests when revising.
